analysis.one_liner: Bans bisphenol A (BPA) in food and drink containers and requires periodic safety reviews of food additives.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 74 House cosponsors, was referred to a committee and its Health subcommittee in March 2009 and never received a vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have treated any food or beverage container made with or releasing bisphenol A — a chemical used in hard plastics and can linings — as an illegal poisonous substance under federal food law, banning it from food packaging. It allowed temporary, renewable waivers for products where no replacement was technologically feasible, but required those products to carry a prominent BPA warning label. It also directed the FDA to periodically re-review substances on the 'generally recognized as safe' list and ban or restrict any later found to cause reproductive or developmental harm, and tightened the safety information manufacturers must submit for new food-contact chemicals.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats canned or packaged food — especially infants, pregnant women, and children, the groups most studied for BPA exposure — would get food containers free of BPA or, where a waiver applied, a clear warning label. Consumers would also benefit from ongoing federal review of food-additive safety as science advances.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, especially infants and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Bans any food or beverage container composed of or releasing bisphenol A, treating it as a container made of a poisonous or deleterious substance under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

Takes effect 180 days after enactment, with only narrow one-year waivers (renewable once) for facilities that show replacing BPA is not technologically feasible — and those waived products must carry a prominent warning label about potential health effects.

Requires the FDA to review, at least every five years, substances on the 'generally recognized as safe' list and remove or restrict any that new evidence shows cause reproductive or developmental toxicity.

Requires — rather than merely permits — manufacturers of food-contact substances to notify the FDA of safety determinations, including whether the substance causes reproductive or developmental toxicity.
Preserves states' rights to adopt stricter BPA rules than the federal standard.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical companies that make bisphenol A and food and beverage companies that rely on BPA-based cans and plastics would bear the cost of reformulating packaging, seeking waivers, and adding warning labels. Some of those costs could show up in prices for canned and packaged foods during the transition.

drawbacks.text: Reformulating packaging on short notice could raise costs for canned and packaged goods, which would be passed partly to consumers, and could strain small food producers who lack the resources of large manufacturers to find substitutes or navigate the waiver process.
The waiver process lets any facility using a waived product continue BPA use for up to two years, so exposure would not end immediately even if the law passed.

Because the ban applies to containers that 'can release' BPA into food, it is a strict standard, and opponents could argue it reaches containers with negligible exposure and lacks a case-by-case health-risk assessment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case was strong: BPA is an endocrine-disrupting chemical and the bill targeted food containers — the main exposure route — with a staged timeline and a narrow waiver system rather than an immediate cliff. The main costs are industry compliance and possibly modest food-price effects during transition, which the 180-day lead time and two-year waiver window were designed to ease. The broader GRAS-review provision would have fixed a known weakness in food-additive oversight, though it also would have expanded FDA's regulatory workload.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2009 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health subcommittee, where it sat and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey of Massachusetts, joined by Rep. Tammy Baldwin, introduced the Ban Poisonous Additives Act of 2009 on March 16, 2009.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction and, the next day, to the committee's Subcommittee on Health.
Seventy-four House members cosponsored the bill — 73 Democrats and 1 Republican — but no further action was recorded in the 111th Congress.
The bill died at the end of the 111th Congress in January 2011 without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bisphenol A producers and food and beverage companies using BPA-lined cans and BPA plastics were better off: no packaging ban was enacted, and no federal requirement for periodic re-review of 'generally recognized as safe' additives was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: BPA makers and food packaging users

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban BPA in food containers and strengthen FDA review of food additives.

for.name: 73 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad support within the majority party.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it was never reported out for a floor vote.

against.name: Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or floor action for the bill in the two years it sat pending.

against.name: Bisphenol A and plastics packaging industry
against.role: Producers of BPA and BPA-based food packaging
against.what_they_did: Had a strong commercial stake in the bill's defeat; no federal BPA packaging ban was enacted during the 111th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with 73 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsor, but its fate was decided in committee, where no recorded vote was ever taken; party positions on the merits were never tested.

industries.industry: Bisphenol A and epoxy resin manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have treated BPA as a poisonous substance in food containers, effectively ending a major market for the chemical. Because the bill died, BPA remained legal in food packaging nationwide.

industries.industry: Food and beverage canners and packaged-food companies
industries.note: The bill would have forced canners and packagers to reformulate packaging within 180 days or seek waivers with warning labels, raising compliance costs that would partly reach shoppers. Its failure left packaging reform voluntary rather than mandated.

industries.industry: Consumers of canned and packaged food
industries.note: With the bill dead, consumers had no federal ban on BPA in food containers and continued bearing any associated exposure risk; no mandatory warning labels or periodic FDA re-review of 'safe' additives resulted.
